newsitem.title: UK: Pick-up in UK housing to buoy growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Pick-up in UK housing to buoy growth in 1997.

text.p: Recovery in Britain's housing market will further boost already buoyant consumption this year but without overheating the economy as in the past, economists say.
Rising interest rates and a debt overhang mean a re-run of the roller-coaster ride in house prices of the late 1980s, which helped to fuel an economic boom, is not on the cards.
"The housing recovery will have an impact on economic growth but...quantitatively it'll be on a different scale to the late 80s," said UBS economist and housing expert Rob Thomas.
Two-thirds of Britons own their own homes, so a healthy property market is crucial for consumer confidence.
"A strong housing market is hugely important in the UK," said Bank of America economist Jeremy Hawkins. "It increases confidence and leads to a greater willingness to spend."

"Most people are relatively optimistic about housing in 1997. If we continue to see the momentum in the last few months being maintained, then it will turn out that assumptions put together a few months ago for GDP this year are too low."
The government is forecasting fairly robust GDP (gross domestic product) growth of 3.5 percent this year.
Rapid housing turnover boosts sales of durable goods as new home owners fill their property with furniture and "white goods", such as cookers and refrigerators.
Thomas said most of the fall-out from this increase in consumption had already been built into growth forecasts, but added there was a slight danger it would exceed expectations.

"If house prices rise by more than expected, which is quite possible...the economy could be much more buoyant than we are anticipating, particularly going into next year and the year after when we've got things slowing down," he said.
Predictions of rising house prices to the turn of the century have reignited demand among Britons keen to jump on the property bandwagon before it gains speed.
Britain's largest mortgage lender, the Halifax building society, has predicted house prices will rise up to eight percent in 1997, compared with around seven percent in 1996.
Thomas, who expects house prices to rise 10 percent both this year and next, said the impact on the economy of this increase would be muted.
"There was a lot of leakage of mortgage equity withdrawal in the 1980s -- borrowing to finance consumption -- and that is not happening at the moment," he said.
Against the trend of the 1980s, households have been net injectors of cash into their homes, cutting their debt. "I do expect that to turn around, but not in a big way," Thomas said.
Households were starting off with a higher level of debt this time, which would also reduce their propensity to borrow.

He estimated that Britain's housing stock was worth around a trillion pounds and mortgage debt is more than 400 billion ($675 billion). "So close on 40 percent of housing stock is mortgaged, which is a vastly higher rate than in the late '80s," he said.
Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc, said people who lived through the aftermath of the 1980s might think twice about over-extending themselves.
Interest rates are widely expected to rise this year as the government tries to hold down inflation. This should help to curb excessive demand, economists say, but to a limited extent.
Official interest rates are expected to rise to around seven percent by the end of the year from their present six percent.

But the lure of capital gains on property will take some of the sting off higher rates. "Trying to puncture the housing boom over the next few years will be very difficult to do," said Thomas. -- London newsroom +44 171 542 7708 ($1=.5922 Pound)
